nameStory: The Atlantic surf clam gets its name from where beachcombers most often encounter it – washed up in the surf zone after storms. Also called the 'hen clam' for its impressive size, this giant of the clam world earned the nickname 'skimmer' from commercial fishermen who harvest them by skimming large dredges across the sandy ocean floor.
description: The Atlantic surf clam is a massive saltwater clam that's one of the largest bivalves you'll find along New England's coast. These impressive mollusks can grow between 7.9 and 8.9 inches long, making them much bigger than most other clams in our waters. Their thick, sturdy shells are oval-shaped and built to withstand the pounding surf where they live. You'll most commonly spot their empty shells washed up on beaches after storms, where they've become favorite sand-digging tools and natural beach treasures for generations of beachgoers.

idTips.label: Shell Size
idTips.description: Impressively large shells reaching 7-9 inches long – about the size of a dinner plate and much bigger than any other clam shell you'll find on New England beaches

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Thick, heavy, oval-shaped shell that feels solid and substantial in your hands, like holding a piece of smooth stone

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Smooth exterior surface that may feel slightly chalky when dry, with concentric growth rings visible as subtle ridges you can run your finger across

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: Exterior ranges from pale gray to yellowish-brown, often bleached white by sun and surf, while the interior is typically glossy white or cream

idTips.label: Hinge Area
idTips.description: Prominent triangular hinge area with a deep pit (chondrophore) that held the internal ligament – look for this distinctive spoon-shaped depression

habitat: Atlantic surf clams live buried in sandy and muddy bottoms of the continental shelf, typically 10-100 feet underwater off New England's coast. You won't find living clams on the beach – they spend their lives completely submerged in offshore waters. However, their large, distinctive shells regularly wash ashore on sandy beaches throughout the region, especially after storms stir up the ocean floor.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells begin washing ashore more frequently as spring storms churn up offshore waters. Fresh shells may still have some of their natural coloration.
seasonality.summer: Peak time to find shells on beaches as summer storms and increased wave action bring them to shore. Living clams are reproducing in the warm offshore waters during late summer.
seasonality.fall: Excellent season for shell collecting as fall storms create ideal conditions for shells to wash up. Shells found now may be bleached white from summer sun exposure.
seasonality.winter: Winter storms can deposit large numbers of shells on beaches, though they may be partially buried by shifting sands. Cold weather makes the shells feel especially solid and heavy.

funFact: These clam shells are so perfectly shaped and sized that they've been used as natural sand shovels, ashtrays, soap dishes, and even serving bowls for generations – making them one of the most repurposed natural objects found on New England beaches!
confusionNotes: The large size alone distinguishes surf clam shells from other common beach finds like quahogs, razor clams, or scallops. If you can hold it comfortably in both hands and it's oval-shaped, it's almost certainly a surf clam shell. Remember: 'If it's huge, it's probably a surf clam' – no other clam shells on New England beaches come close to this size.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Atlantic surf clam,' these animals actually live well offshore in deeper waters and never inhabit the actual surf zone. The name comes from where we encounter their shells, not where the living animals are found. This is one of the most commercially important shellfish species in the region, though most harvesting happens far from shore.
compareHints: Since this is the only Spisula species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other large bivalves in the region. Surf clam shells are much larger and thicker than quahog shells, lack the distinctive 'ears' of sea scallops, and are more oval than the elongated razor clam shells. The combination of massive size, oval shape, and thick walls makes surf clams unmistakable among New England's marine bivalves.
